name: Olga Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Olga. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the city centre team, around Central Station and the shopping streets. A lot of it is shoplifting, lost phones, people sleeping in the station doorways, and tourists who've had their bag taken. I'm two years in and, honestly, I'm better with the screen than with the shouting part. My tutor constable told me my report writing is great but I freeze a bit when a fight kicks off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use an AI app to translate for tourists on the spot, and at home I use one to quiz me for the law exams. The force has a report drafting tool and I was one of the first to try it. Half the older officers think I'm a bit of a nerd, which is fair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, money and so on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat on Weaver Street with a friend from school who works in a call centre. I've got about two thousand on a credit card from when my car died, and maybe two weeks of money saved. Our pay as junior constables is the bottom of the scale, so I'm careful, but careful doesn't stretch far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I thought the tools would make the boring bits faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a reminder that the problems in policing are people problems: not enough officers, not enough mental health support, not enough housing for the people in the station doorways. Online I'd probably share something about rules for police use of facial recognition, because even small AI can do harm. At work I'd keep showing people the translation app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means my edge with the tools stays small. My job is safe enough, but I'm still on the bottom pay step with a credit card I can't clear, and my flatmate's call centre keeps talking about closing. If she loses her job, I can't cover the rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on patrol and work on the part I'm weak at, the confrontation side, maybe ask to go on the public order refresher. I'd pay the credit card down a hundred a month even if it means fewer nights out. And I'd keep studying for the economic crime unit exam, because fraud is where my head works best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit restless. I want things to move, and they wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your flatmate's call centre might close. How would that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hit me hard. The rent's eleven hundred between us, and I couldn't do it alone on my pay. I'd have to find another flatmate fast or go back to my dad's, which is forty minutes from the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you freeze when a fight kicks off. What happened the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two men were going at each other outside the station bar, and I stood there a second too long working out what to say. My tutor got between them before I moved. Nobody was hurt, but I went home and wrote down everything I should have done, like a homework list.

say: Policing problems are **people problems**: officers, mental health support and housing.
Even small AI needs **rules on facial recognition** by police.
think: My **edge with the tools** would stay small if AI stays modest.
If my **flatmate's call centre** closes, I can't cover the rent alone.
do: Ask for the **public order refresher** to fix her weak spot on the street.
Pay the **credit card** down a hundred a month.
Keep studying for the **economic crime unit** exam.
feel: **Restless** and slightly disappointed that nothing would move.
S0.quote: I went home and wrote down everything I should have done, like a homework list.
fieldNote: She is **strong on screens** and weak on confrontation, the reverse of many colleagues.
Her money risk runs through **her flatmate's job**, not her own.
Even when AI stalls, she pushes for **rules on police AI** use.

steps.text: Ask her sergeant for a place on the public order refresher
Pay the credit card down a hundred a month
Study for the economic crime unit entry exam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I kind of expect. It's already happening in bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to give officers more street time and less screen time, but only with strong rules. I'd post about bias in predictive policing, because I've read the studies. At the station I'd volunteer to help train people on the new tools, and I'd say so loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me in the short run and maybe bad later. Right now I'm the junior who can actually use the tools, so I'd be useful. But the fraud and economic crime work I want is mostly desk work, checking bank records and writing case files, and that's exactly the thinking work the card says goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up as a tools champion at the station and ask for the course to count toward my development review. I'd still go for the economic crime unit, but I'd focus on interviewing victims and suspects, the part where a human matters. I'd start a small side thing, helping older people in my building set up scam alerts on their phones, for a few pounds a visit, if the force signs it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy at the same time. I'm good at the thing that's changing, which isn't the same as being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd need the force to approve a side job. Would you actually ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd fill in the business interest form properly. You don't mess around with that as a police officer. It's maybe sixty a month, but sixty a month clears the credit card a lot faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The civilian investigators in the fraud office. Most of what they do is going through bank statements, and an AI will read a year of statements in a minute. My friend Tomasz is one of them, and he's got two kids.

say: AI could give officers **more street time**, but only with strong rules.
I'd post about **bias in predictive policing** and volunteer to train colleagues.
think: Being the junior who **can use the tools** helps me now.
The **economic crime desk work** I want is exactly what goes first.
do: Sign up as the station's **tools champion** and count it toward her review.
Aim for **victim and suspect interviews** within economic crime work.
Start helping neighbours with **scam alerts** for a few pounds, with force approval.
feel: **Excited and uneasy** together; good at what's changing isn't the same as safe.
S1.quote: I'm good at the thing that's changing, which isn't the same as being safe.
fieldNote: She spots that her **career plan points into** the most exposed corner.
Adaptive but careful: **side income** only with official approval.
Her **progressive concern** about bias runs alongside eager use of tools.

steps.text: Become the station's champion for the new AI tools
Target interview work within the economic crime unit
Set up scam alerts for older neighbours for small fees
Post and campaign about bias in predictive policing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. My tool skills stop being special almost overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need laws now, before AI decides who gets stopped and searched. I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for public oversight and probably go to a protest, in my own time. At work I'd say the human side of policing is the part to protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being good with AI doesn't help when AI doesn't need a helper. By 2028 the case files, the statements, the fraud checks are all done by the system, so the economic crime unit I've been studying for basically disappears. What's left is the street, which is the part I'm weakest at. And robots for that come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the economic crime exam and put everything into the street side: the public order course, more nights on the busy team, getting good at the part that lasts three more years. I'd pay off the credit card fast, using the side money, and stop all extras. And I'd look at jobs where AI would need a person to check it, like auditing police AI systems, if those exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like I trained for the wrong match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come around 2031. What does that three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd be swapping the job I'm good at for the job I'm bad at, just to get three more years. That's a weird bargain at twenty-nine. But three years of pay is three years of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmate that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her both of us need a plan, because her call centre goes in the first wave. We'd probably sit with a spreadsheet, two months of rent between us, and work out who moves out first if it comes to that.

say: We need **laws now**, before AI decides who gets stopped and searched.
The **human side** of policing is the part to protect.
think: Being good with AI **stops mattering** when AI no longer needs a helper.
What's left is **the street**, the part where I'm weakest.
do: Drop the **economic crime exam** and focus on public order skills.
Clear the **credit card** fast using side money and cut all extras.
Look for jobs **auditing police AI** systems if they exist.
feel: **Unsettled**, as if she trained for the wrong match.
S2.quote: I'd be swapping the job I'm good at for the job I'm bad at, just to get three more years.
fieldNote: The fast case **wipes out her edge**; adaptability becomes a scramble.
She uses the **three-year gap** practically, even against her strengths.
Shared rent ties her to **her flatmate's call centre** job, which goes first.

steps.text: Switch focus from economic crime to the public order team
Clear the two-thousand credit card using side money
Join a campaign for public oversight of police AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. That's enough time to be clever about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window for unions and lawmakers to write the rules, and I'd push the federation to get involved. Online I'd share guides for officers on using AI well. At work I'd keep being the tools person, but with a purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years lets me ride the wave for a while and then step off. I'd be valuable for two or three years helping roll the tools out, and that's a story for a CV. After that, I need to be somewhere AI needs a human for, like checking how the system treats people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the force's AI working group, if there is one, and if there isn't, I'd ask to start one. I'd do an evening course in data ethics or digital investigation, online, paid in instalments. I'd keep the scam-alert side work going and grow it into something bigger, maybe training for community centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a worry I keep poking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry you keep poking at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm helping build the thing that replaces my mates. If I'm on the working group, I'm in the room when they decide how many officers a shift needs. I don't know if I'd say yes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for an evening course on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Instalments, maybe forty a month, and I'd ask the force to cover half as development. The scam-alert work would pay the rest. It's tight, but five years gives me room to do it slowly.

say: This is the **window for rules**, and the federation must get involved.
I'd share guides for officers on **using AI well**.
think: I'd **ride the wave** for two or three years, then step off.
Later I need work where AI **needs a human**, like checking fairness.
do: Ask to join or start the force's **AI working group**.
Take an evening course in **digital investigation** at about forty a month.
Grow the **scam-alert work** into training for community centres.
feel: **Mostly hopeful**, with a worry she keeps poking at.
S3.quote: If I'm on the working group, I'm in the room when they decide how many officers a shift needs.
fieldNote: Five years turns her into a **planner**, using the rollout as a CV story.
Her guilt about **replacing colleagues** is the sharpest moment here.
Money still shapes everything: **instalments** and half-funding from the force.

steps.text: Join or start the force's AI working group
Take an evening digital investigation course in instalments
Run scam-awareness training for local community centres
Push the federation to help write police AI rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. A decade. I'd be thirty-seven. That's practically a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse not to. I'd be the one at the station saying let's plan, not panic. Online I'd keep sharing things about rights and oversight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'd have time to get properly good on the street and to build a second skill in digital investigation or AI oversight. The worry is just that I'm broke now, and ten years of bottom-of-the-scale pay doesn't build a cushion on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the economic crime exam after all, but plan to move from it within five years toward oversight work. I'd clear the credit card this year and then save fifty a month, nothing heroic. And I'd keep the side work small and steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. A bit impatient, because I like things to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell yourself in 2036 one thing now, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't get so attached to being the tech person that you forget how to talk to people. In the end the thing that lasts is being the officer someone trusts at three in the morning. Machines might get there, but I'd want to be there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date, 2039, change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. By 2039 I'd want to be off the street anyway, doing oversight or training. If I'm still on patrol at forty, something went wrong.

say: We have time to do this **fairly**, so there's no excuse not to.
I'd be the one saying **plan, not panic**, at the station.
think: Ten years **suits me**, with time for street skills and a second skill.
I'm **broke now**, and bottom-scale pay won't build a cushion alone.
do: Take the **economic crime exam** and plan to move toward oversight work.
Clear the **credit card** this year, then save fifty a month.
Keep the **side work** small and steady.
feel: **Calm-ish** and a bit impatient for things to move.
S4.quote: In the end the thing that lasts is being the officer someone trusts at three in the morning.
fieldNote: With a decade, her adaptability turns into a **two-track plan**.
Her reminder to herself is about **people skills**, not tech.
Money remains the **soft spot** even in the calmest case.

steps.text: Take the economic crime exam, then move toward AI oversight
Clear the credit card, then save fifty a month
Keep the scam-alert visits going at a steady pace

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd panic, but because my whole plan gets flipped and I'd have no money to cushion it. What would help is the force paying for retraining as part of the job, and proper public jobs in AI oversight that people like me could move into. And honestly, a way to clear small debts so they don't decide everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who checks the machines. Everyone talks about whether we keep our jobs. Nobody asks who's checking whether the AI treats a kid from Weaver Street the same as a kid from the nice end of town. That should be a job for a human.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who's checking whether the AI treats a kid from Weaver Street the same as a kid from the nice end of town.
portrait: A **27-year-old city centre officer**, two years in, sharing a flat on Weaver Street with a friend.
Uses **AI tools daily**, but freezes in fights, the opposite of many street officers.
Carries a **credit card debt** and two weeks of savings, with rent tied to her flatmate's call centre job.
Moves fast and plans hard, but sees that the fast cases **flip her edge** into a weakness.
Cares most about **fair oversight** of police AI and wants that to become her future job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her plan flips and she has no money to cushion it.
whatWouldHelp: **Force-paid retraining** and real public jobs in **AI oversight**.
Help to clear **small debts** so they don't decide everything.
